Chapter 3: Focus and Commitment — Choosing What Matters Most
Ever notice how one of the toughest things for any organization isn’t what to do—but what not to do? Let’s be honest, with limited time and resources, trying to chase every good idea almost always leads to, well, mediocrity.
That’s where the OKR framework really shines. It forces us to focus—to home in and commit to just a handful of high-impact goals, instead of scattering our energy everywhere.
Here’s where the discipline of focus truly begins: with some tough choices. Leaders and teams alike have to ask themselves, "What are those few things that, if we nailed them, would make the biggest difference?" That usually means saying “no” to a lot of good ideas, so we can say a confident “yes” to the best ones.
OKRs help you sharpen that focus in a few simple but powerful ways.
First, they encourage you to set a small number of objectives—usually just three to five. Doesn’t sound like much, right? But that’s the point. This limit actually frees people up from feeling like they have to do everything at once. It’s liberating.
Next, OKRs make those objectives visible to everyone. When the top priorities are out in the open, it becomes a lot easier for teams to align their efforts—and avoid duplicating work.
And because OKRs are reviewed and updated regularly—typically every quarter—teams have a natural rhythm for reflecting on what’s working, making adjustments, and recommitting to what matters most.
But here’s something to pay attention to: Focus isn’t just about picking goals. It’s about truly committing to them. Once OKRs are set, they become your north star for every decision. Teams use them to guide daily work, figure out where to put resources, and even sort out conflicts when they come up.
So, when a shiny new opportunity appears, the first question is, "Does this help us move toward our current objectives?" If not, maybe it needs to wait.
Now, this level of commitment takes courage. It means letting go of pet projects, challenging the status quo, and holding yourself—and each other—accountable for results. That’s not always easy. But the payoff? It’s huge. When everyone’s pulling in the same direction, progress really starts to pick up speed.
Let me share a quick real-world example. Imagine a tech company facing fierce competition. For years, they tried to juggle a bunch of product lines at once, but it just wasn’t working. Once they adopted OKRs, they pinpointed the one product with the most potential—and made it their top priority. Every team, from engineering to sales to customer support, aligned their key results around this single goal. And you know what happened? Innovation sped up, morale shot higher, and the product launch was a big success.
So, here’s the key takeaway: Focus and commitment aren’t just buzzwords—they’re daily habits. OKRs give you the structure to build those habits, so your best intentions can actually become real action.
